en: The Sūtra on the Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Great Vidyā of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha, Spoken by the Buddha,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by imperial decree. At that time,
the World-Honored One was in Tuṣita Heaven,
gathered in one place together with countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of bodhisattvas.
At that time, there were countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, namely:
Sātāgiri, Hemavata, Nandikeśvara, Maheśvara, Maheśvaravejayanta, Nārāyaṇa, and others.
Furthermore, there were countless devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all the stellar deities.
When this assembly had thus all gathered together at the Buddha’s gathering,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One.”
Now there are all manner of rākṣasas who roam the world, causing great terror;
we pray only that the World-Honored One will have compassion for the world and eliminate this fear.
He spoke the great mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha,
so as to cause those rākṣasas and all the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others,
including all the planetary deities who act to one's disadvantage, [to be subdued].
Upon seeing that great radiance, they all became bewildered and faint, fleeing in terror;
they were unable to cause harm to any sentient beings.
World-Honored One, is it only these multitudes who become terrified upon seeing it?
Even Śakra loses his majestic power;
all those māra-obstacles that manifest as great wrathful and malevolent forms are utterly destroyed.
He is unable to harm any sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
Bhagavān, now is the very time. Why?
Because all the Māras and their like are present in this assembly.
We pray that the Bhagavān will proclaim the great mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called "The Universally Blazing Light of Great Wrath.
Having entered this samādhi, he...
Immediately, he emitted a great radiance from his eyes,
manifesting in various colors;
that light shone universally upon all worlds.
Having shone forth, [the light] returned and remained before the Buddha like a great mass of fire.
Then, from within that light, a great wrathful body was manifested;
with blazing flames and a most fierce appearance, it stood before the Buddha.
Those who see it are struck with fear.
All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth [are likewise terrified].
And all the powers of every bhūta are utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
As I have requested, please grant this teaching so that practitioners of the recitation in the future may achieve success in all their endeavors.
All bhūtas will be completely subdued;
whatever is sought shall be granted,
and even hidden treasures within the earth shall all be obtained.
O Bhagavān, by the power of the majesty and virtue of this great vidyā-mantra,
may it subdue and influence all humans and non-humans alike,
causing them to enter a state of awakening and perform song and dance.
Furthermore, as for serving as their attendants, there was nothing they did not comply with;
even when their bodies were dismembered to serve as food, they did not dare to disobey.
O World-Honored One, such is the power of this Great Mantra.
Even insentient things such as mountains and stones, when [the Buddha’s] power descends upon them,
can be shaken and made to manifest signs of awakening;
how much more so for all the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans?
If any among such multitudes should act in opposition, they shall all have their heads split asunder.
At that time, the manifested wrathful image,
in a single kṣaṇa, manifests a bodily radiance that shines like the sun.
Standing before the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, he then uttered the great vidyā-mantra of Vajragandha: Namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye. Ma...

At that time, after the emanated wrathful image had spoken this great mantra,
he further spoke the great mantras and various methods of accomplishment for the Bodhisattva Vajragandha.
If one uses this illumination to empower and burn安息香 (anxiang, *agaru* or *karpūra*),
it can cause all beings to awaken; furthermore,
it can completely dispel and resolve all states of possession by devas, humans, yakṣas, and even by malevolent spirits such as *chi-mei*.
Furthermore, the practitioner recites this vidyā before an image of Maheśvara.
He then contemplates the image with a wrathful expression and bathes the image with the five kinds of pure water.
Furthermore, use white sandalwood to prepare an unguent with which to anoint the body of the deity’s image.
Make offerings of various fragrant flowers,
and while pressing both hands upon the image, recite the Great Mantra.
From the first watch of the night until dawn, the sound of his recitation continued without ceasing.
Then, the Great Lord Maheśvara, having certainly manifested a transformation body in the form of a non-Buddhist ascetic,
came before the reciter and stood there in silence.
Upon seeing it, the reciter immediately prostrated and said,
"Noble One, welcome!
The emanated image replied, "Welcome, welcome!"
The reciter shall then seek whatever they desire;
the deity will immediately grant their wishes, and all shall be obtained.
The deity’s image is given to the practitioner.
Once the vow has vanished and is no longer manifest,
the practitioner attains siddhi; thereafter,
all actions performed will be accomplished according to one's wishes.
Whether one performs the rites of pacification, augmentation, magnetizing, subjugation, or summoning, they will certainly be accomplished.
For the rite of pacification, one should use *gomaya* that has not fallen to the ground.
Having drawn the four-sided maṇḍala,
once it is completed, take a single silver bowl and first grind white sandalwood to prepare the unguent.
Smear the inside and outside of the bowl thoroughly with [the ointment],
then fill it with pure water and place it within the maṇḍala.
Recite the great mantra one hundred and eight times.
When one empowers that bowl, the bowl immediately awakens;
it may rise and leave the altar, or move or tremble, indicating that the dharma has been accomplished.
One should then sprinkle this water upon the crown of the person's head or have them drink it.
All calamities shall be extinguished.
If this water is sprinkled upon cities, towns, and villages,
the calamities of the people therein shall all be stilled.
All sentient beings shall obtain benefit.
Furthermore, if one acts as a pacifier for kings and great military hosts, [the following shall be performed].
One should perform the homa by mixing together curd, white sesame seeds, white non-glutinous rice, cow’s milk, and so forth;
for every recitation of the Great Mantra, one should utter the name of the King.
Alternatively, perform one thousand *homa* offerings;
the calamities affecting the king and his military host will all be pacified.
Furthermore, there is another method: either paint the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha white.
As a sign of raining down the nectar of immortality upon sentient beings,
one should recite the Great Mantra three times each day before this image while further visualizing it.
Once this has been realized before one, one subsequently recites the syllable *HŪṂ*.
All calamities and misfortunes will then cease and be extinguished.
Even if there should be enemies who come to harass or oppress one, [they shall be subdued].
One should perform homa with cow’s milk while reciting the great mantra one thousand times;
thus, enemies will naturally disperse and calamities will be extinguished.
Alternatively, one may use frankincense, white sesame seeds, and clarified butter.
Performing homa in this manner pacifies all calamities.
Furthermore, as for the method for performing the rite of augmentation (puṣṭi),
one should paint a great rākṣasī.
The body is yellow in color and has sixteen arms,
each holding various objects;
it is adorned with all manner of exquisite ornaments.
Once the painted image has been completed,
one should make offerings with various incenses and flowers;
before this image, one should recite the great vidyā-mantra without ceasing.
When the rākṣasī herself appears,
one may summon all yakṣas, rākṣasas, and their retinues;
she can fulfill all the practitioner’s requests for wealth and grain.
One can also extract treasures hidden within the earth and use them as one desires.
Furthermore, paint the image of a yakṣa white in color,
and likewise prepare a fragrant unguent using white-colored incense.
Anoint the body of that image with white flowers as an offering.
Before this image, recite the Great Mantra aloud while holding white flowers in one's hand;
for each recitation, cast one flower to strike the body of the image.
If one recites the vidyā eight thousand times over the course of three periods during seven days,
that yakṣa will appear and become a servant to the reciter.
They all dared not disobey his commands and served him;
at times they personally delivered all manner of wealth and treasures,
or brought forth hidden hoards from within the earth.
This shall cause the reciter to attain great wealth and prosperity.
Furthermore, to perform the rite of magnetizing (*vaśīkaraṇa*),
one should paint an image of the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā.
The body is red in color and has twelve arms,
each holding an object;
it is adorned with exquisite celestial garments.
Once the painted image has been completed,
the practitioner performs visualization before the image,
visualizing the body of the painted image emitting a great red light.
In a single instant, it illuminates the three realms;
all the devas, nāgas, and rākṣasas therein,
as well as all humans and non-humans, will be filled with reverence and affection.
Once the visualization has been perfected, one may then seek the desired objective.
If a practitioner wishes to seek reverence and love,
they should first recite the Great Mantra one thousand times.
However, one should fashion an image of him from red sandalwood wood and place it before an image of the Bodhisattva Vajragandha.
The practitioner should then take karavīra flowers.
Before an image of the Bodhisattva,
recite the great mantra once, utter his name once,
and cast [the object] toward the image; repeat this until the recitation is completed seven times.
One will certainly attain their veneration and affection.
Furthermore, as for the ritual application: fashion images of a man and woman, or images of a boy and a girl, using auspicious wood (śrīvṛkṣa).
Reciting his name while casting white mustard seeds upon his image, one will certainly achieve the state of being held in reverence and affection within seven days and nights.
Furthermore, there is another method: mix white mustard seeds with white sandalwood.
Recite the Great Mantra eight hundred thousand times;
this will cause all people to hold one in the highest esteem and attain universal respect and affection.
Furthermore, as for the method if one wishes to [deal with] an enemy:
For one who has lost their mind and is deranged,
one should use human bone to fashion a vajra-kila eight finger-widths in length.
Burn安息香 (benzoin) and beef together to fumigate the ritual stake.
Bury it before the gate of the enemy's house;
within three days, that person will lose their mind, leave home, and run about frantically.
Alternatively, one may mix beef, dog meat, and cow urine to form a clay paste.
Fashioning an image of the enemy, one should place it within a śītavana charnel ground;
the enemy, along with all their retinue, will then depart beyond a thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, if one wishes to cause an enemy to leave their native land,
one should likewise fashion a vajra-kila from human bone,
wrap it with thread dyed with human blood, and encircle the kila.
Strike upon the head of Maheśvara.
The practitioner should step upon the deity Maheśvara with his left foot on either the fourteenth or the eighth day of the lunar month.
The practitioner recites the Great Mantra without ceasing until that deity utters a great cry of suffering;
the enemy then loses their mind and falls into a state of frantic madness.
Together with their retinues, they emerge from the wilderness like a herd of wild beasts.
Furthermore, for one who wishes to utterly destroy enemies through the Dharma,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Vajragandha.
His body is black in color and has a hundred arms, manifesting a wrathful aspect.

In his hands he holds various weapons, including banners, vajras, mallets, nooses, tridents, swords, bows, arrows, battle-axes, great axes, bone clubs, vajra-hooks, withered corpses, human heads, and skulls.
Furthermore, his body is adorned with hundreds of thousands of exquisite ornaments;
he emits a great radiance surpassing that of the sun and moon,
manifesting the form of one who destroys all enemies.
All those yakṣas and rākṣasas,
as well as all the great and malevolent spirits and ghosts,
were utterly shattered, struck with terror, and fled in all directions.
If one wishes to destroy an enemy, even unto death,
the practitioner should first recite the Great Mantra eight thousand times.
Thereafter, one should fashion a vajra-kila from human bone, two finger-widths in length.
Maintaining a wrathful state of mind without ceasing day or night,
recite the Great Mantra eight thousand times.
Once the ritual stakes have been consecrated, [proceed].
Using beef as clay, fashion an effigy of the enemy eight finger-widths in length.
Use the aforementioned stake to nail it to the crown of its head, or to its mouth, flanks, ears, or navel.
Alternatively, if [the mantra] is applied to the torso, knees, feet,
or other such parts, after one week the body of that enemy will certainly be destroyed,
like the branches of an *ari* tree.
It can even destroy all great evils.
Furthermore, for the rite of destroying an extremely formidable enemy:
take cow urine, salt, and vinegar, boil them together until they form a paste.
Mix it with the *gomaya* (cow dung) or *kuśa* grass of a pure land to fashion the image of an enemy. Then,
smear white mustard seeds all over that image.
Roast it over a fire;
when the enemy falls ill, they will certainly die.
Furthermore, there is a method using khadira wood.
Fashion a stake eight finger-widths long;
empower it eight hundred times,
and while reciting the name of the enemy, nail it into their effigy.
In an instant, he will bind himself by his own power.
Alternatively, one may fashion an image of the enemy using human ash and create a vajra-stake from human bone.
By nailing that person's body parts, they shall suffer from fever until their death.
Furthermore, there is a method: fashion a nail of iron two finger-widths long, empower it one hundred times with mantras, and bury it outside the gate of the enemy.
Within three days, one will certainly leave one's home.
Alternatively, bury the aforementioned stake within a temple of Maheśvara;
at the time of burial, call out the name of the enemy.
He will immediately become possessed by the deity Maheśvara;
or his name shall be invoked while he is buried within an empty house, whereupon he will immediately become possessed by a piśāca;
or one may take the froth from the mouth of a black snake and smear it inside a fired earthen vessel.
This will cause the enemy to eat it and die instantly.
Another method is to fashion a bone-stick out of iron six finger-widths long;
first, one should call out the name of the enemy.
Recite the Great Mantra seven times.
Consecrate the incense of *an-shi-xiang* (安息香) and burn it over the bone splinters;
bury them within the house of the enemy.
That person will immediately experience great suffering and distress;
however, if they go outside, the suffering caused by the bone-thorns will be relieved.
Furthermore, there is another method: use *nimba* wood to fashion a stake twelve finger-widths long.
Strike the three places—the head, the arms, and the flanks—and call out the name.
Furthermore, use ox hair as incense and burn it while calling out the name.
Thus, that person shall be liberated from the possession of the mother-demon (*mātṛ-graha*).
Furthermore, there is another method: using *ariṣṭa* wood to fashion an image of the enemy,
and writing their actual name within its belly.
He uses human bone to fashion nails and drives them into three places: the head, the arms, and the sides.
Thereupon, he suffers intense pain.
If the nail remains as it was before,
another method is to fashion an image of the enemy out of *gomaya* (cow dung).
One should coat the entire body of the image with white mustard seeds while reciting the Great Mantra until the image dries.
Bury [the remains] in a śītavana forest.
Above it, recite the Great Mantra eight hundred times and empower white mustard seeds, scattering them over the site.
Whatever the practitioner seeks shall all be accomplished.
Furthermore, the ritual is the same as before:
fashion an image and smear it with the three types of meat—human, ox, and dog—along with white mustard seeds.
He places the enemy within his own house,
whereupon the enemy becomes utterly deluded and never enters the house again.
Furthermore, if the practitioner wishes to summon a female ghost (*yakṣiṇī*) in the present life:
Go to a śītavana charnel ground;
mix poison, salt, and blood together,
and perform homa while reciting the Great Mantra.
After three periods of three days had passed,
at night, a female ghost appeared within the homa fire-pit;
her appearance was upright and beautiful, and she shone with brilliant light.
She stood before the practitioner.
The practitioner then prepared white food, sacrificial offerings, *argha* water, and so forth.
At that time, the female spirit said, "I am extremely hungry."
The practitioner immediately replies, "I have already prepared it for you.
He then produces food, *arghya*, and so forth, and gives them, saying:
"In accordance with the Buddha’s command, accept these as you please."
Once the female ghost had received the food,
she said to the practitioner:
"Whatever you seek, I shall cause you to achieve it all."
When the female ghost had finished speaking, she immediately vanished from sight.
Next, the method for binding by means of a spell is explained:
one should fashion an image of the adversary using yellow orpiment.
Having smeared the body of the image and the vajra with ashes from a funeral pyre,
the practitioner should step upon the vajra with his left foot and step upon that image with his right foot while reciting the great mantra.
In a brief moment, the enemies and their retinues lose their minds,
become deranged, and depart from their original location.
Next, the method for banishing enemies is explained.
The practitioner first recites the great mantra one hundred times.
Thereafter, they visualize the fundamental subtle syllable,
which transforms into a camel.
Furthermore, visualize the preceding syllable mounted upon that camel.
Again, imagine a person striking that enemy with a bone ladle.
Then, visualize yourself within a wind-wheel.
Sit facing south and recite the syllable "Phu.
Do not cease the sound of the recitation until the adversary has vanished and no longer appears.
This visualization practice can even dispatch Vajrasattva,
let alone an enemy.
If one uses white mustard seeds mixed with frankincense, [the result will be achieved].
For one who performs *homa* while reciting the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) one hundred times,
all enemies will swiftly depart from their original locations.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment (*siddhi*) is explained:
First, the practitioner should draw the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā in red color upon a piece of silk or a skull; however,
they should not draw an image of an enemy under her feet to be trampled.
The practitioner assumes a wrathful form and recites the great mantra without ceasing.
Furthermore, using thorny wood, white mustard seeds, and salt, he performs a homa sacrifice;
the enemy will swiftly lose their mind and fall into madness.
Furthermore, according to another method,
one should use human blood mixed with blue pigment to paint the image of the enemy upon a piece of blue silk.
The practitioner should perform this on either the eighth or the seventh day.
At the time of midnight, he prepared food for an offering.
When someone came to receive this food,
they said to the practitioner, "What shall we have us do?"
At that time, the practitioner shall repay the enemy with the same coin.
Furthermore, assuming an expression of wrath, he shall utter the name of the enemy while reciting the Great Mantra and performing homa.
Upon reaching the seventh day, the victim will immediately perish and die.
Furthermore, there is a rite in which one fashions an image of the enemy out of *nimba* wood and cuts it into pieces.
Use *nimba* wood specifically as fuel;
perform the homa together with the body of the image.
Recite the great mantra once for each piece burned, and the bodies of those enemies will be destroyed.
Furthermore, in a śītavana cemetery,
collect flower garlands and burn agalloch incense;
recite the Great Mantra eight hundred times to empower those garlands.
Scatter it at the house of an enemy;
they, along with their kinsmen, will all suffer from a three-day fever.
Alternatively, bury the garland before the door of an enemy.
That enemy will swiftly meet their end.
Alternatively, one may burn *agaru* (sandalwood) incense and fumigate beef,
using this meat to perform *homa*.
Recite the great mantra once and call the name of the enemy once;
throw [the substance] into the fire for three nights,
and that enemy will immediately suffer from a four-day malaria fever.
If one wishes to release [the affliction], perform a homa using breast milk;
it will then be restored to its former state.
Furthermore, another method is to smear the maṇḍala with funeral ashes.
Furthermore, fashion an image of the enemy using human bone ash;
place it within the maṇḍala and strike that image with red flowers.
Recite [the mantra] once and cast [the effigy] once for three days;
then cast the image into the fire,
and the body of that enemy will immediately be destroyed.

Furthermore, the method for performing the rite of subjugation through binding is as follows:
First, paint the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā.
Her body is of a yellow hue and perfectly formed,
emitting great radiance that illuminates the realm of space.
Standing upon the summit of a great mountain, one treads upon the image of the enemy.
The practitioner performs visualization before this image until it appears before them.
All enemies shall be completely bound and restrained.
Furthermore, there is another method:
on a cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should depict the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā exactly as described previously.
Make offerings with exquisite incense and flowers.
Use realgar and pure earth mixed with water to fashion an image of the enemy.
The practitioner, before the bodhisattva’s painting,
holds a five-pronged vajra in his hand,
assumes a wrathful expression, and rises to trample upon his enemies.
Recite the great mantra one thousand times;
all enemies will be completely suppressed and subdued.
Furthermore, there is another method: fashion an image of the enemy using yellow wax.
The practitioner steps with his left foot and again performs visualization:
he visualizes that enemy within a range of hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
and further visualizes that noble beings fill the entirety of space.
Once this visualization has appeared before one,
those enemies will naturally become like fools and be unable to cause harm.
If this method of accomplishment is directed toward the Buddhas, [the result is even greater].
Even the Buddhas do not wish to contravene this,
let alone all the sages, worthies, humans, and non-humans.
He then spoke the Great Mantra for Subjugation:
Oṃ namo bhagavate mahāvajragandhārimahāmāla-senāpate lala la saṃbhava sarvadeva...
*Ṭhuṃ ṣaṇśāśaya sphoṭaya vidārapaya sarvanāśaya sarvaduṣṭān nigṛhṇa mama sarva...*

form two vajra-fists with both hands.

with both hands, form the vajra-pañjali;

And there were countless devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, along with the lunar mansions and planets.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they received and believed his teaching with reverence, prostrated themselves, and withdrew.
*The Sūtra on the Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of Vajragandha Bodhisattva*, Scroll Lower.
